verses.text: In the first year of King Cyrus of Persia, the LORD stirred up Cyrus’s spirit so the word he’d spoken through Jeremiah would come true. Cyrus sent a proclamation across his kingdom and put it in writing:
“Here’s what Cyrus, king of Persia, says: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms on earth. He’s told me to build him a house in Jerusalem in Judah.
If you belong to his people, may your God be with you. Go up to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel. He is God, and his house belongs in Jerusalem.
Wherever any of his people are still living, their neighbors should help them out with silver, gold, goods, and animals, in addition to what they freely give for God’s house in Jerusalem.’”
Then the family heads of Judah and Benjamin, the priests, and the Levites got ready to go build the LORD’s house in Jerusalem. These were all the people whose spirits God had stirred up to go.
Their neighbors backed them up with silver vessels, gold, goods, animals, and valuables, on top of everything else they gave freely.
Cyrus also brought out the vessels from the LORD’s house that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and put in the house of his gods.
Cyrus, king of Persia, had Mithredath the treasurer bring them out and count them out for Sheshbazzar, prince of Judah.
Here’s the count: thirty gold platters, a thousand silver platters, twenty-nine knives,
thirty gold bowls, four hundred ten silver bowls of a second kind, and a thousand other vessels.
Altogether there were five thousand four hundred gold and silver vessels. Sheshbazzar brought them all up when the captives went from Babylon to Jerusalem.

These are the people of the province who came home out of exile. King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had hauled them off to Babylon, and now they made it back to Jerusalem and Judah, each to their own town.
They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. Here’s the count of the men of Israel:
Parosh’s descendants: 2,172.
Shephatiah’s descendants: 372.
Arah’s descendants: 775.
Pahathmoab’s descendants, from the lines of Jeshua and Joab: 2,812.
Elam’s descendants: 1,254.
Zattu’s descendants: 945.
Zaccai’s descendants: 760.
Bani’s descendants: 642.
Bebai’s descendants: 623.
Azgad’s descendants: 1,222.
Adonikam’s descendants: 666.
Bigvai’s descendants: 2,056.
Adin’s descendants: 454.
Ater’s descendants from Hezekiah’s line: 98.
Bezai’s descendants: 323.
Jorah’s descendants: 112.
Hashum’s descendants: 223.
Gibbar’s descendants: 95.
People from Bethlehem: 123.
Men from Netophah: 56.
Men from Anathoth: 128.
People from Azmaveth: 42.
People from Kiriath Arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth: 743.
People from Ramah and Geba: 621.
Men from Michmas: 122.
Men from Bethel and Ai: 223.
People from Nebo: 52.
People from Magbish: 156.
The other Elam’s descendants: 1,254.
Harim’s descendants: 320.
People from Lod, Hadid, and Ono: 725.
People from Jericho: 345.
People from Senaah: 3,630.
Here are the priests: Jedaiah’s descendants from Jeshua’s family: 973.
Immer’s descendants: 1,052.
Pashhur’s descendants: 1,247.
Harim’s descendants: 1,017.
The Levites were the descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel from Hodaviah’s line: 74.
The singers were Asaph’s descendants: 128.
The gatekeepers’ descendants came from the families of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai: 139 in all.
The temple servants came from these families: Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth,
Keros, Siaha, Padon,
Lebanah, Hagabah, Akkub,
Hagab, Shamlai, Hanan,
Giddel, Gahar, Reaiah,
Rezin, Nekoda, Gazzam,
Uzza, Paseah, Besai,
Asnah, Meunim, Nephisim,
Bakbuk, Hakupha, Harhur,
Bazluth, Mehida, Harsha,
Barkos, Sisera, Temah,
Neziah, and Hatipha.
The descendants of Solomon’s servants came from these families: Sotai, Hassophereth, Peruda,
Jaalah, Darkon, Giddel,
Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth Hazzebaim, and Ami.
Altogether there were 392 temple servants and descendants of Solomon’s servants.
The following people came up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer. They couldn’t show from their family lines or ancestry whether they belonged to Israel:
The descendants of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda: 652.
From the priestly families there were the descendants of Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai. Barzillai had married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and taken their family name.
They looked for their names in the family records but couldn’t find them. So they were counted ineligible and removed from the priesthood.
The governor told them they couldn’t eat any of the most holy things until a priest was there to serve with the Urim and Thummim.
The whole group added up to 42,360,
plus 7,337 male and female servants. They also had 200 singers, men and women.
They had 736 horses and 245 mules,
435 camels and 6,720 donkeys.
When they got to the LORD’s house in Jerusalem, some of the family heads gave freely to rebuild God’s house on its old site.
They gave what they could to the treasury for the work: 61,000 gold darics, 5,000 silver minas, and 100 sets of priests’ clothes.
The priests, Levites, some of the people, the singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants settled in their towns. All Israel settled in their own towns.
By the time the seventh month came, the Israelites were in their towns. Then the people came together in Jerusalem, united as one.

Jeshua son of Jozadak got to work with his fellow priests, along with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his relatives. They built the altar of the God of Israel so they could offer burnt offerings there, just as it was written in the law of Moses, the man of God.
They were scared of the peoples around them, but they set the altar on its base anyway. There they made burnt offerings to the LORD every morning and evening.
They celebrated the Festival of Booths as written, bringing the required number of burnt offerings each day, just as the rule for that day called for.
After that came the regular burnt offering, the offerings for the new moons and all the LORD’s appointed holy festivals, and the gifts people freely chose to offer to the LORD.
They started giving burnt offerings to the LORD on the first day of the seventh month. The foundation of the LORD’s temple still hadn’t been laid.
They paid the stoneworkers and carpenters. They gave food, drink, and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar from Lebanon by sea to Joppa, as King Cyrus of Persia had authorized.

In the second month of the second year after they came to God’s house in Jerusalem, the work got underway. Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Jeshua son of Jozadak, their fellow priests and Levites, and everyone who’d come back to Jerusalem from exile started the work. They put Levites twenty and older in charge of the work on the LORD’s house.

Jeshua stood with his sons and brothers, along with Kadmiel and his sons, the descendants of Judah. They supervised the workers in God’s house together with Henadad’s sons, their sons, and their fellow Levites.

When the builders laid the foundation of the LORD’s temple, the priests took their places in their robes with trumpets. The Levites descended from Asaph held cymbals. They were there to praise the LORD as King David of Israel had directed.

They sang back and forth, praising and thanking the LORD: “He is good! His faithful love for Israel lasts forever!” Then everybody let out a huge shout of praise to the LORD because the foundation of his house was in place.
But many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads had seen the first house. When they saw the foundation of this house being laid, they cried out loud. Many others shouted for joy.
Nobody could tell the sound of the cheering from the sound of the crying. The people were so loud that you could hear them far away.
Judah and Benjamin’s enemies heard that the people who’d come back from exile were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel.
They went to Zerubbabel and the family heads and said, “Let us build with you. We seek your God just like you do. We’ve been sacrificing to him since Esar Haddon, king of Assyria, brought us here.”

But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of Israel’s family heads told them, “You have no part with us in building a house for our God. We’ll build it ourselves, together, for the LORD, the God of Israel, just as King Cyrus of Persia told us to.”
Then the people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make it hard for them to build.
They hired advisers to work against them and wreck their plans throughout the reign of King Cyrus of Persia, right up to the reign of King Darius of Persia.
At the start of Ahasuerus’s reign, they wrote an accusation against the people of Judah and Jerusalem.
In Artaxerxes’s time, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of their companions wrote to King Artaxerxes of Persia. The letter was written in Syrian script and sent in the Syrian language.
Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes making a case against Jerusalem. Here’s how it went.
It came from Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions: the Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites, Archevites, Babylonians, Shushanchites, Dehaites, and Elamites,
and the other peoples the great and noble Osnappar had brought over and settled in the city of Samaria and elsewhere in the country beyond the River, and so on.
Here’s a copy of the letter they sent: “To King Artaxerxes, from your servants, the people beyond the River.

The king should know that the Jews who came up from your territory have arrived here in Jerusalem. They’re rebuilding that wicked, rebellious city. They’ve finished the walls and repaired the foundations.
The king should also know that if the city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, they won’t pay tribute, customs duties, or tolls. In the end, that will hurt the kings.
Since we eat the salt of the palace and can’t just stand by while the king is dishonored, we’re sending word to let you know.

Have someone search the records of your ancestors. You’ll find in those records that this city is rebellious and has caused trouble for kings and provinces. There have been uprisings there before. That’s why the city was destroyed.
We’re telling the king that if the city is rebuilt and the walls are finished, you won’t have any territory left beyond the River.”
The king sent this reply to Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions living in Samaria and elsewhere beyond the River: “Peace.
The letter you sent us has been read to me clearly.
I ordered a search. It turned up that this city has risen up against kings in the past and that there have been rebellions and revolts there.
Powerful kings have also ruled Jerusalem and governed the whole country beyond the River. People paid them tribute, customs duties, and tolls.
Issue an order now to stop these men. The city is to stay unbuilt until I give the order.
See to it right away. Why let the damage grow and hurt the kings?”
When the copy of King Artaxerxes’s letter was read to Rehum, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they rushed to the Jews in Jerusalem and used armed force to make them stop.
So the work on God’s house in Jerusalem came to a halt. It stayed that way until the second year of King Darius of Persia’s reign.
The prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo spoke to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel.
Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak got up and started building God’s house in Jerusalem. God’s prophets were right there helping them.
Around that time Tattenai, governor beyond the River, came with Shetharbozenai and their companions. They asked, “Who gave you the order to build this house and finish this wall?”
They also asked for the names of the men putting up the building.
But their God was watching over the Jewish elders. The officials didn’t make them stop while the matter went to Darius and they waited for his written reply.
Here’s a copy of the letter to King Darius from Tattenai, governor beyond the River, Shetharbozenai, and his companions, the Apharsachites who lived beyond the River.
The letter they sent him said, “To King Darius, wishing you every peace.

The king should know that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. They’re building it with large stones and setting timbers into the walls. They’re working hard, and the job is going well.
We asked the elders, ‘Who gave you the order to build this house and finish this wall?’
We also asked their names so we could write down who was leading them and let you know.
Here’s the answer they gave us: ‘We’re servants of the God of heaven and earth. We’re rebuilding the house that stood here many years ago, the one a great king of Israel built and finished.
But our ancestors provoked the God of heaven to anger. He handed them over to Nebuchadnezzar the Chaldean, king of Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar destroyed this house and took the people away to Babylon.
Then in the first year of Cyrus as king of Babylon, King Cyrus issued an order to rebuild this house of God.

Nebuchadnezzar had taken the gold and silver vessels from God’s house, moving them from the temple in Jerusalem to the temple in Babylon. King Cyrus took them back out of the temple in Babylon and had them handed over to Sheshbazzar, whom he’d appointed governor.
He told him, “Take these vessels and put them in the temple in Jerusalem. Have God’s house built on its own site.”
That same Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of God’s house in Jerusalem. Work has gone on since then, but the house still isn’t finished.’

So now, if it pleases the king, please have someone search the royal treasury in Babylon to see whether King Cyrus actually issued an order to rebuild this house of God in Jerusalem. Please send us your decision on the matter.”
King Darius issued an order, and they searched the archives in Babylon where the treasures were kept.
They found a scroll at Achmetha, in the palace in the province of Media. Here’s what it recorded:

In his first year as king, Cyrus issued this order about God’s house in Jerusalem: Rebuild the house, the place where sacrifices are offered, and lay a solid foundation. It is to be sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide,
with three layers of large stones and a layer of new timber. The royal household is to pay the expenses.

Return the gold and silver vessels from God’s house that Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem to Babylon. Bring them back to the temple in Jerusalem and put each one in its place in God’s house.
So now, Tattenai, governor beyond the River, Shetharbozenai, and your Apharsachite companions beyond the River, stay well away from there.
Leave the work on this house of God alone. Let the Jewish governor and elders rebuild God’s house on its own site.
I’m also ordering you to help these Jewish elders rebuild God’s house. Pay their expenses promptly from the royal funds collected as tribute beyond the River so nothing holds them up.

Give them whatever they need every single day, as the priests in Jerusalem direct: young bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, as well as wheat, salt, wine, and oil. Don’t miss a day.
Then they can offer sacrifices with a pleasing aroma to the God of heaven and pray for the lives of the king and his sons.

I also order that if anyone changes this decree, a beam is to be pulled out of their house. They’re to be lifted up and fastened to it, and their house is to be turned into a dung heap because of what they did.
May the God who made his name dwell there overthrow any king or people who try to change this decree or destroy his house in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have issued this order. Get it done without delay.
Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, Shetharbozenai, and their companions carried it out promptly because King Darius had sent the order.

The Jewish elders kept building, and the work went well through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo. They finished the building as the God of Israel had commanded and as Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes king of Persia had decreed.
They finished the house on the third day of Adar in the sixth year of King Darius’s reign.
The Israelites, the priests, the Levites, and the rest of those who’d returned from exile celebrated the dedication of God’s house with joy.
To dedicate God’s house, they offered one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, and four hundred lambs. For a sin offering for all Israel, they brought twelve male goats, one for each tribe of Israel.
They assigned the priests and Levites to their groups for serving God in Jerusalem, just as it’s written in the book of Moses.
Those who’d come back from exile celebrated Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month.

The priests and Levites had purified themselves together, so they were all clean. They slaughtered the Passover animals for everyone who’d returned from exile, for their fellow priests, and for themselves.
The Israelites who’d returned from exile ate the meal. So did everyone who’d joined them after turning away from the unclean practices of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel.

They joyfully celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days. The LORD had given them that joy by turning the heart of the king of Assyria toward them so he would give them a hand with the work on the house of God, the God of Israel.
After all this, while Artaxerxes was king of Persia, there was Ezra son of Seraiah, whose line went back through Azariah and Hilkiah,
then Shallum, Zadok, and Ahitub,
then Amariah, Azariah, and Meraioth,
then Zerahiah, Uzzi, and Bukki,
then Abishua, Phinehas, Eleazar, and Aaron the chief priest.

That’s the Ezra who went up from Babylon. He was a scribe who knew the law of Moses, which the LORD, the God of Israel, had given. The king granted everything he asked for because the hand of the LORD his God was on him.
In King Artaxerxes’s seventh year, some Israelites went up to Jerusalem, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants.
Ezra reached Jerusalem in the fifth month of the king’s seventh year.
He set out from Babylon on the first day of the first month and reached Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month. The good hand of his God was on him.
Ezra had set his heart on studying the LORD’s law, living it out, and teaching its statutes and rulings in Israel.
Here’s a copy of the letter King Artaxerxes gave Ezra. Ezra was a priest and a scribe trained in the words of the LORD’s commands and statutes for Israel:
“Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, scribe of the law of the perfect God of heaven. Now,
I’m issuing this order: Any Israelites, priests, or Levites in my kingdom who freely choose to go to Jerusalem may go with you.
The king and his seven advisers are sending you to look into affairs in Judah and Jerusalem according to the law of your God that’s in your hands.
You’re also to carry the silver and gold the king and his advisers freely offered to the God of Israel, whose home is in Jerusalem.
Take all the silver and gold you find throughout the province of Babylon, along with what the people and priests freely give for the house of their God in Jerusalem.
Be quick to use this money to buy bulls, rams, and lambs, along with their grain offerings and drink offerings. Offer them on the altar at your God’s house in Jerusalem.
Use the rest of the silver and gold however you and your fellow Israelites think best, in keeping with your God’s will.
Hand over the vessels you’ve been given for service at your God’s house in the presence of the God of Jerusalem.
If you need to provide anything else for your God’s house, pay for it out of the royal treasury.
I myself, King Artaxerxes, order all the treasurers beyond the River to provide promptly whatever Ezra the priest and scribe of the law of the God of heaven asks of you,
up to one hundred talents of silver, one hundred cors of wheat, one hundred baths of wine, and one hundred baths of oil. No limit is set for salt.
Whatever the God of heaven commands, do it exactly for his house. Why bring wrath on the realm of the king and his sons?
We also make it clear that no tribute, customs duty, or toll may be charged to any priest, Levite, singer, gatekeeper, temple servant, or worker at this house of God.
And you, Ezra, use the wisdom your God has given you to appoint magistrates and judges. They’re to judge the people beyond the River who know your God’s laws. Teach anyone who doesn’t know them.
If anyone refuses to obey your God’s law and the king’s law, carry out the sentence promptly, whether it’s death, banishment, loss of property, or prison.”
Bless the LORD, the God of our ancestors! He put it in the king’s heart to make the LORD’s house in Jerusalem beautiful.
He also showed me faithful love before the king, his advisers, and all his powerful officials. The hand of the LORD my God on me gave me strength, and I gathered leaders from Israel to go up with me.
Here are the family heads and the family lines of those who came up with me from Babylon while Artaxerxes was king:
From Phinehas’s descendants, Gershom. From Ithamar’s, Daniel. From David’s, Hattush.
From Shecaniah’s descendants, from Parosh’s line, Zechariah, with 150 men listed with him in the family records.
From Pahathmoab’s descendants, Eliehoenai son of Zerahiah, with 200 men.
From Shecaniah’s descendants, the son of Jahaziel, with 300 men.
From Adin’s descendants, Ebed son of Jonathan, with 50 men.
From Elam’s descendants, Jeshaiah son of Athaliah, with 70 men.
From Shephatiah’s descendants, Zebadiah son of Michael, with 80 men.
From Joab’s descendants, Obadiah son of Jehiel, with 218 men.
From Shelomith’s descendants, the son of Josiphiah, with 160 men.
From Bebai’s descendants, Zechariah son of Bebai, with 28 men.
From Azgad’s descendants, Johanan son of Hakkatan, with 110 men.
From Adonikam’s descendants, the last ones were Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, with 60 men.
From Bigvai’s descendants, Uthai and Zabbud, with 70 men.
I brought them together at the river that flows to Ahava, and we camped there for three days. I looked over the people and the priests and realized there wasn’t a single descendant of Levi there.
So I sent for the leaders Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, and for the teachers Joiarib and Elnathan.
I sent them to Iddo, the leader at Casiphia. I told them what to say to Iddo and his fellow temple servants there so they’d bring us people to serve at our God’s house.
Our God’s good hand was on us, so they brought us Sherebiah, a man with good judgment from the line of Mahli son of Levi, son of Israel. He came with his sons and brothers, eighteen in all.
They also brought Hashabiah and, with him, Jeshaiah from Merari’s descendants, along with his brothers and their sons, twenty in all.
They brought 220 temple servants from the group David and his officials had assigned to help the Levites. Every one was listed by name.
Right there at the Ahava River I called for a fast. We wanted to humble ourselves before our God and ask him for a clear way ahead for us, our little ones, and everything we owned.

I felt ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen to protect us from enemies on the road. We’d already told him, “Our God’s hand is on everyone who seeks him, to do them good. His power and anger are against everyone who turns away from him.”
So we fasted and begged our God to help us, and he answered our request.
Then I picked out twelve of the leading priests: Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers.
I weighed out the silver, gold, and vessels for them. These were the offerings for our God’s house from the king, his advisers and officials, and all the Israelites who were there.
I handed over 650 talents of silver, silver vessels weighing 100 talents, and 100 talents of gold,
along with twenty gold bowls weighing a thousand darics and two vessels of fine, shiny bronze, as precious as gold.
I told them, “You’re set apart for the LORD, and these vessels are set apart too. The silver and gold are gifts freely given to the LORD, the God of your ancestors.
Keep watch over them until you weigh them in Jerusalem in the rooms of the LORD’s house, in front of the leading priests, the Levites, and the heads of Israel’s families.”
So the priests and Levites took charge of the weighed silver, gold, and vessels to bring them to our God’s house in Jerusalem.
On the twelfth day of the first month, we left the Ahava River for Jerusalem. Our God’s hand was on us. He rescued us from enemies and bandits along the way.
We reached Jerusalem and stayed there for three days.

On the fourth day, we weighed the silver, gold, and vessels in our God’s house and handed them to Meremoth son of Uriah the priest. With him was Eleazar son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui.
Everything was counted and weighed, and all the weights were written down right then.

The people who’d returned from exile brought burnt offerings to the God of Israel: twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve male goats for a sin offering. All this went up as a burnt offering to the LORD.
They delivered the king’s orders to his local governors and to the governors beyond the River. So those officials supported the people and God’s house.

After all this, the officials came to me and said, “The people of Israel, the priests, and the Levites haven’t kept apart from the peoples of the lands. They’ve followed the detestable practices of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites.

They’ve taken daughters from those peoples as wives for themselves and their sons, so the descendants set apart for God have mixed with the peoples of the lands. The officials and rulers have led the way in this wrong.”
When I heard that, I tore my clothes and my robe, pulled hair from my head and beard, and sat down in shock.
Everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me because of what the returned exiles had done. I sat there stunned until the evening offering.
At the evening offering, I got up from where I’d been sitting in humiliation, with my clothes and robe still torn. I dropped to my knees and held out my hands to the LORD my God.
I said, “My God, I’m too ashamed and embarrassed to lift my face to you. Our wrongdoing has piled up over our heads, and our guilt reaches all the way to heaven.

We’ve been deeply guilty from our ancestors’ days right up to today. Because of our wrongdoing, we, our kings, and our priests were handed over to the kings of other lands, to the sword, exile, plunder, and public shame. That’s where we are today.

But now, for this brief moment, the LORD our God has shown us grace. He’s let some of us escape and given us a foothold in his holy place, so our God can brighten our eyes and give us a little new life in our bondage.

We’re still in bondage, but our God hasn’t abandoned us there. He’s shown us faithful love in the sight of the Persian kings, giving us new life so we can raise up our God’s house, rebuild its ruins, and have a wall in Judah and Jerusalem.
“And now, our God, what can we say after all this? We walked away from your commands,

the ones you gave through your servants the prophets: ‘The land you’re going to take possession of is unclean because of the peoples who live there. Their detestable practices have filled it from one end to the other with uncleanness.

So don’t give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons. Don’t ever seek their peace or prosperity. Then you can stay strong, enjoy what the land produces, and leave it to your children as their inheritance forever.’
“After everything that’s happened to us for the evil we did and the guilt we brought on ourselves, you, our God, have punished us less than we deserved and let this group survive.
Are we really going to break your commands again and join ourselves to the peoples who do these detestable things? Wouldn’t you be angry enough to wipe us out, with no one left and nobody escaping?
LORD, God of Israel, you’re righteous. Some of us have escaped and are still here today. Here we stand before you with all our guilt, though no one can stand before you because of it.”

Ezra was praying and confessing, crying and throwing himself down in front of God’s house. A huge crowd of Israelites gathered around him, men, women, and children, and the people broke down in tears.
Shecaniah son of Jehiel, one of Elam’s descendants, answered Ezra, “We’ve wronged our God by marrying foreign women from the peoples of the land. Even now there’s hope for Israel in this.

So let’s make a covenant with our God to send away all these wives and the children born to them. Let’s follow your counsel, my lord, and the counsel of those who tremble at our God’s command. Let it be done according to the law.
Get up. This is yours to handle, and we’re with you. Take courage and do it.”
Ezra got up and made the leading priests, the Levites, and all Israel swear they’d do what had been proposed. And they swore.

Then Ezra got up from in front of God’s house and went into the room of Jehohanan son of Eliashib. Once inside, he ate no food and drank no water. He was grieving over the wrong the returned exiles had done.
They announced throughout Judah and Jerusalem that all the returned exiles had to gather in Jerusalem.
Following the officials’ and elders’ advice, anyone who didn’t show up within three days would lose everything they owned and be put out of the assembly of returned exiles.

Within the three days, all the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered in Jerusalem. It was the twentieth day of the ninth month. Everyone sat in the square in front of God’s house, shaking over what was happening and because of the pouring rain.
Ezra the priest stood up and told them, “You’ve done wrong by marrying foreign women and adding to Israel’s guilt.
Now confess to the LORD, the God of your ancestors, and do what pleases him. Separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from the foreign women.”
The whole assembly answered loudly, “We have to do what you’ve told us to do.
But there are a lot of us, and the rain is heavy. We can’t stand outside. This won’t be sorted out in a day or two, because we’ve done great wrong in this matter.

Let our officials act for the whole assembly. Everyone in our towns who’s married a foreign woman should come at a set time with their town’s elders and judges. Let’s do this until our God’s fierce anger turns away from us and the matter is resolved.”
Only Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah stood against this. Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite backed them up.

The returned exiles carried out the plan. Ezra the priest and certain family heads were appointed by name to represent their ancestral families. On the first day of the tenth month, they sat down to look into the matter.
By the first day of the first month they’d finished dealing with all the men who had married foreign women.
Here are the men from priestly families found to have married foreign women. From the family of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah.
They pledged to send away their wives. As they were guilty, they offered a ram from the flock for their guilt.
From Immer’s descendants: Hanani and Zebadiah.
From Harim’s descendants: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah.
From Pashhur’s descendants: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah.
From the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah, also called Kelita, Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.
From the singers: Eliashib. From the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri.
From the rest of Israel, from Parosh’s descendants: Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Malchijah, and Benaiah.
From Elam’s descendants: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah.
From Zattu’s descendants: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza.
From Bebai’s descendants: Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai.
From Bani’s descendants: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth.
From Pahathmoab’s descendants: Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh.
From Harim’s descendants: Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Shimeon,
Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah.
From Hashum’s descendants: Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.
From Bani’s descendants: Maadai, Amram, Uel,
Benaiah, Bedeiah, Cheluhi,
Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib,
Mattaniah, Mattenai, Jaasu,
Bani, Binnui, Shimei,
Shelemiah, Nathan, Adaiah,
Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai,
Azarel, Shelemiah, Shemariah,
Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph.
From Nebo’s descendants: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Iddo, Joel, and Benaiah.
All these men had married foreign women. Some had children with their wives.
